title: Cryonics: Hi, Frozen Body!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore cryonics, the practice of preserving human bodies or brains at extremely low temperatures in hopes of future revival. They cover its origins with Robert Ettinger and his book The Prospect of Immortality, the first suspension cases (Ettinger, James Bedford), the difference between vitrification and freezing, the idea that death is a gradual process, and the procedure from deathbed stabilization through glycol-based cryoprotectant perfusion to storage in liquid nitrogen. They discuss Alcor membership costs, the Cryonics Institute, neuropatients, criticism from scientists and skeptics, religious and legal questions (including new birth certificates), the history of galvanic reanimation and Frankenstein, animal reanimation research, the bankruptcy-era abandonment of bodies, and Ted Williams's suspension and the family dispute over it. The episode closes with listener mail and a Facebook/Twitter call for stories.

segments.title: Opening and the Simpsons frozen body episode
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode title, reference a Simpsons episode with a frozen body, and note the recent death of Robert Ettinger, who founded cryonics.

segments.title: Origins of cryonics and vitrification
segments.summary: Ettinger's book The Prospect of Immortality led to the first suspension within three years. Early cases included Ettinger and James Bedford. The hosts distinguish vitrification from freezing and discuss the roughly ten-thousand-year limit set by cosmic rays. Walt Disney rumor is dismissed.

segments.title: Death as a process and hypothermia research
segments.summary: Alcor's view that death is a gradual process, with some brain function remaining after the heart stops. Hypothermia research on heart attack patients shows gradual cooling and rewarming can prevent oxygen-related cell damage.

segments.title: Membership fees and costs
segments.summary: Alcor membership fees by family relationship and student status, plus the cost of body and neuro suspension and the surcharge for non-members.

segments.title: Other cryonics groups
segments.summary: Besides Alcor, there is the Michigan-based Cryonics Institute, founded by Robert Ettinger, whose website the hosts joke about.

segments.title: The suspension procedure
segments.summary: The process from deathbed to facility: stabilizing circulation, using heparin, removing water from cells, perfusing cryoprotectant, cooling to around negative 130 degrees Celsius, then storage in liquid nitrogen, with neuropatients stored head-down.

segments.title: Skepticism, pseudoscience and the reanimation question
segments.summary: Critics call cryonics pseudoscience. Cryobiologists avoid endorsing it for reputational reasons. Organizations admit they cannot yet reanimate anyone and rely on future nanotechnology.

segments.title: Galvanic reanimation history and animal research
segments.summary: Nineteenth-century galvanic reanimation of executed criminals and its link to Frankenstein. Modern research: a rabbit kidney vitrified and revived, a nematode revived, and dog and monkey blood replaced with antifreeze.

segments.title: Legal, ethical and religious issues
segments.summary: Legal status of suspended people, a possible new birth certificate, Arizona bill that would have put Alcor under the funeral board, religious perspectives, and the abandonment of bodies by bankrupt companies in earlier decades. Alcor's trust fund and finances are discussed.

segments.title: Ted Williams and popularity of cryonics
segments.summary: Ted Williams's suspension, the family dispute over his DNA and cremation wishes, and Alcor's member and patient counts. A short mention of an Errol Morris film about cryonics.

segments.title: Listener mail and outro
segments.summary: Listener stories about a tick removed from a child's ear, a split uvula, and an engagement, plus calls for stories via Facebook, Twitter, and email. The episode closes with a promo for the video podcast Stuff from the Future.
